about: Thin-period fill, batch 1 of 2: the 20 wanted gap items before 300 CE (Ram picked them 2026-11-20).

events.name: Stonehenge's Sarsen Circle Raised
events.date_display: c. 2600–2400 BCE (the site itself is older, from c. 3000 BCE)
events.description: On Salisbury Plain in southern England, Neolithic builders raise the great sarsen stones of Stonehenge: a ring of uprights capped with lintels, enclosing five giant trilithons. Many sarsens weigh over twenty tonnes and were dragged about twenty-five kilometres; the smaller bluestones had been brought from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
events.note: English Heritage dates the sarsen phase to c. 2500 BCE; the ditch and bank are c. 3000 BCE. Sarsen source (West Woods, ~25 km) from Nash et al. 2020.
events.significance: Stonehenge's stones frame the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, showing that Neolithic farming communities could organise labour on a huge scale and follow the sun's yearly cycle. It became one of the world's best-known prehistoric monuments, and its purpose is still debated.

events.name: Code of Ur-Nammu Issued in Sumer
events.date_display: c. 2100–2050 BCE (middle chronology; issued by Ur-Nammu or his son Shulgi)
events.description: In the Sumerian city of Ur, a king of the Third Dynasty of Ur issues a collection of laws written on clay tablets. Many of its rules set fixed fines in silver for injuries rather than physical punishment. It is the oldest law code whose text survives, older than Hammurabi's.
events.note: Ur-Nammu reigned c. 2112–2095 BCE (middle chronology); some scholars credit the code to his son Shulgi, so the name says 'Code of Ur-Nammu' (its conventional name) rather than 'Ur-Nammu issues'. Renamed from the gap-list wording for that reason.
events.significance: The code shows that written law, with penalties set by the state, was already established in Sumer centuries before Hammurabi. It belongs to a Mesopotamian legal tradition that later codes, including Hammurabi's, continued and expanded.

events.name: First Palace Built at Knossos
events.date_display: c. 2000–1900 BCE (the first palace; rebuilt after an earthquake c. 1700 BCE)
events.description: On the island of Crete, the Minoans build the first palace at Knossos, a great complex of storerooms, workshops and halls arranged around a central court. It becomes the largest centre of the Minoan civilization, Europe's earliest palace-based society, later famous for its colourful frescoes and advanced drains.
events.note: Protopalatial period begins c. 1900 BCE; the visible ruins are mostly from the rebuilt palace. The labyrinth legend is left out (only a suggested connection).
events.significance: Knossos shows that a literate state with long-distance trade had arisen in Europe by the early second millennium BCE. The Minoans influenced the Mycenaean Greeks, who later took over the palace, and Arthur Evans's excavations from 1900 shaped modern ideas of Bronze Age Europe.

events.name: Hatshepsut Becomes Pharaoh
events.date_display: c. 1473 BCE (regent from c. 1479; crowned about seven years later)
events.description: Hatshepsut, widow of Thutmose II and regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, has herself crowned king of Egypt. Ruling as pharaoh, often shown in the regalia of a male king, she sponsors great building works, including her temple at Deir el-Bahari, and a trading expedition to the land of Punt.
events.note: The gap list said c. 1479, but that is the start of her regency; she was crowned c. 1473 (Shaw: reign c. 1473–1458). Year moved to 1473 for accuracy.
events.significance: Hatshepsut ruled for about two decades of peace and prosperity, one of the few women to hold full royal power in ancient Egypt. After her death many of her images were defaced and her name left off king lists, and she was largely forgotten until Egyptologists pieced her reign back together.

events.name: Rigveda Composed
events.date_display: c. 1500–1200 BCE (composed over centuries and passed down orally)
events.description: In the northwest of the Indian subcontinent, poet-priests compose the hymns of the Rigveda, over a thousand Sanskrit hymns to gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna. Memorised and recited with great precision, they are passed down orally for many centuries before being written down.
events.note: A process over centuries, not one year (some scholars say c. 1700–1100 BCE). Recommend DateFlow-only (manage.py dateflow-only) so it isn't a guessing question.
events.significance: The Rigveda is the oldest text of Hinduism and one of the oldest in any Indo-European language. Its hymns and rituals shaped later Vedic religion and Hindu practice, and it remains a key source for the language, society and beliefs of early South Asia.

events.name: Akhenaten Elevates the Aten Above Egypt's Gods
events.date_display: c. 1353–1346 BCE (early in his reign, c. 1353–1336)
events.description: The pharaoh Amenhotep IV renames himself Akhenaten and makes the Aten, the disc of the sun, the centre of Egypt's state religion, closing temples of other gods such as Amun. He builds a new capital at Amarna, where royal art takes on a strikingly new and informal style.
events.note: Renamed from the gap-list 'Introduces the Worship of the Aten': the Aten was worshipped before him; he raised it above all other gods. Whether this was true monotheism is debated.
events.significance: Akhenaten's religious revolution is one of the earliest known attempts to centre a state's worship on a single god, though whether it was true monotheism is debated. It was reversed soon after his death, under Tutankhamun, and later kings tried to erase him from the record.

events.name: Battle of Kadesh
events.date_display: c. 1274 BCE (the most widely used date)
events.description: Near the city of Kadesh in western Syria, the Egyptian army of Ramesses II clashes with the Hittite army of Muwatalli II in one of the largest chariot battles ever fought. Ramesses narrowly escapes an ambush; both sides claim victory, but neither takes control of the region.
events.note: Year 5 of Ramesses II, c. 1274 BCE in the usual chronology. The Egyptian accounts are royal propaganda; the result was a stalemate.
events.significance: Kadesh is one of the best-documented battles of the ancient world, recorded in Egyptian texts and temple reliefs and in Hittite letters. Its stalemate was followed, about fifteen years later, by the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, one of the earliest peace treaties whose text survives.

events.name: Oracle-Bone Writing Appears in Shang China
events.date_display: c. 1250 BCE (the earliest inscriptions, from the reign of Wu Ding)
events.description: At the Shang capital near modern Anyang, diviners for King Wu Ding carve questions to the ancestors on turtle shells and ox shoulder blades, then crack them with heat and read the answers. These inscriptions are the earliest known Chinese writing, ancestors of the characters still used today.
events.note: Earliest securely dated inscriptions from Wu Ding's reign (c. 1250–1192 BCE); a mature script, so writing may be older. First recognised in 1899.
events.significance: The oracle bones are the oldest known Chinese writing and the main record of the Shang state, confirming kings named in much later histories. Their script is directly ancestral to modern Chinese characters, one of the longest continuous writing traditions in the world.

events.name: Lapita Voyagers Settle Remote Oceania
events.date_display: c. 1100–800 BCE (Vanuatu c. 1000; Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by c. 800 BCE)
events.description: Seafarers of the Lapita culture, known for their finely stamped pottery, sail east from the islands off New Guinea into Remote Oceania. In sailing canoes they cross wide stretches of open sea to settle Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, islands no human had reached before.
events.note: A process over two or three centuries (radiocarbon). Recommend DateFlow-only. Countries VU, FJ, TO, WS, PG are new to the countries table (add-country before loading).
events.significance: The Lapita voyages were the first human crossings of truly open ocean, far beyond sight of land. Their descendants in Tonga and Samoa became the ancestral Polynesians, who later settled the rest of the Pacific, from Hawaii to New Zealand and Rapa Nui.

events.name: Carthage Founded
events.date_display: 814 BCE by tradition; the earliest remains date from the late 9th century BCE
events.description: Phoenician settlers from the city of Tyre found Carthage on the coast of modern Tunisia; its name means 'new city'. Greek and Roman legend credits the founding to Queen Dido. Commanding the narrows between Sicily and Africa, it grows into a wealthy trading power with colonies across the western Mediterranean.
events.note: 814 BCE is from the Greek historian Timaeus; archaeology supports a foundation in the late 9th century BCE. The Dido story is legend, and the description says so.
events.significance: Carthage became the leading power of the western Mediterranean, spreading Phoenician trade, language and religion from Sicily to Spain. Its rivalry with Rome led to the three Punic Wars, which ended with the city's destruction and Rome's dominance of the whole region.

events.name: Library of Alexandria Founded
events.date_display: c. 300–285 BCE (under Ptolemy I or Ptolemy II; the exact year is unknown)
events.description: In Alexandria, Egypt's new Greek-ruled capital, the Ptolemaic kings found a great library within the Mouseion, a royal institution for scholars. Its librarians set out to collect copies of every book they can find, and it becomes the greatest centre of learning in the Greek world.
events.note: Founding credited to Ptolemy I (advised by Demetrius of Phalerum) or Ptolemy II. Its end was a gradual decline, not one fire: the significance avoids the myth.
events.significance: The library made Alexandria the intellectual capital of the Hellenistic world, where scholars such as Eratosthenes worked and many Greek texts were edited and preserved. Its gradual decline, rather than a single famous fire, made it a lasting symbol of lost knowledge.

events.name: Trung Sisters Lead a Revolt Against Han Rule
events.description: In the Red River delta of northern Vietnam, the sisters Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị lead a rebellion against the Chinese Han governor and drive his forces out. Trưng Trắc rules as queen until a Han army under the general Ma Yuan crushes the revolt about three years later.
events.significance: Although it was crushed, the revolt made the Trưng sisters enduring national heroines in Vietnam, honoured in temples, street names and a yearly festival. They became a lasting symbol of resistance to Chinese rule, which ended only nine centuries later.

events.name: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun Built
events.description: At Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico, builders complete the Pyramid of the Sun, a stepped platform of rubble and earth faced with stone, about sixty-five metres high. It stands beside the city's great avenue above a man-made tunnel, and the temple that once crowned it has vanished.
events.note: Construction is usually dated c. 200 CE. The tunnel beneath was long thought to be a natural cave.
events.significance: The Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest structures of the ancient Americas and a sign of Teotihuacan's power to organise labour and belief. Its name comes from the Aztecs, who found the city in ruins centuries later; what its builders called it is unknown.

spans.name: Caral–Supe Civilization (Norte Chico)
spans.date_display: c. 3000–1800 BCE (radiocarbon dates; the city of Caral c. 2600–2000 BCE)
spans.description: The oldest known urban society in the Americas, on the coast of north-central Peru. Its towns, such as Caral, built platform mounds and sunken plazas, without pottery and with little sign of warfare.
spans.note: Wikipedia now titles it Caral–Supe; 'Norte Chico' is kept in the name so either search finds it.
spans.significance: Caral–Supe shows that cities and monumental building arose in the Andes independently, about as early as in Mesopotamia and Egypt. It overturned the older view that Andean civilization began much later, with the Chavín.

spans.name: Nok Culture
spans.date_display: c. 1500 BCE to the turn of the era; the terracottas from c. 900 BCE
spans.description: A culture of central Nigeria known for its terracotta sculptures of human heads and figures, among the oldest figurative sculpture in Africa south of the Sahara. Its people were also among West Africa's early iron smelters.
spans.note: Dates from the Goethe University Frankfurt research project; iron smelting from about the mid-first millennium BCE.
spans.significance: Nok's terracottas are among the earliest known sculpture in West Africa, and its furnaces show that iron was being smelted in the region by the first millennium BCE. Some art historians see echoes of its style in later art at Ife, though a direct link is debated.

spans.name: Late Bronze Age Collapse
spans.date_display: c. 1200–1150 BCE (some extend it to c. 1225–1100)
spans.description: A few decades in which many states of the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East collapsed: the Hittite Empire and Mycenaean Greece fell, cities such as Ugarit were destroyed, and Egypt lost its empire in the Levant. Its causes, possibly drought, migrations, the Sea Peoples' raids and failing trade, are debated.
spans.note: Causes debated; the description lists them as possibilities, none as the cause.
spans.significance: The collapse ended the Bronze Age world of palaces, scribes and long-distance trade, and Greece lost the art of writing for centuries. In the recovery that followed, iron came into wide use and new peoples, among them the Phoenicians and the Israelites, rose to prominence.

spans.name: Bantu Expansion
spans.date_display: a gradual process: beginnings estimated c. 2000–1000 BCE; Bantu speakers reached southern Africa by c. 300–500 CE
spans.description: The gradual spread of Bantu-speaking farming peoples from the region of modern Cameroon and Nigeria across much of central, eastern and southern Africa. Over many centuries they carried farming, ironworking and the languages now spoken across the southern half of the continent.
spans.note: The span's years are only a frame for a process with fuzzy ends; date_display says so.
spans.significance: The Bantu expansion shaped the language map of Africa: Bantu languages, from Swahili and Lingala to Zulu, are spoken today by hundreds of millions of people. It also spread farming and ironworking across the south of the continent, the base on which later states such as Great Zimbabwe and Kongo grew.

spans.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
spans.description: The Assyrian state of northern Mesopotamia, which from capitals such as Nimrud and Nineveh built the largest empire the world had yet seen, reaching at its height from Egypt to western Iran. The Babylonians and Medes destroyed it, sacking Nineveh in 612 BCE.
spans.note: Conventional dates: from the accession of Adad-nirari II (911) to the fall of Harran (609). Firm from Assyrian eponym lists, so not marked approximate.
spans.significance: Assyria pioneered the methods of a large empire: provinces under appointed governors, a network of roads and royal messengers, and mass deportations of conquered peoples, including the people of the kingdom of Israel. Babylon and Persia inherited much of this system.

spans.name: Teotihuacan
spans.date_display: c. 100 BCE–550 CE (its decline and the burning of its centre are dated within decades)
spans.description: The great city of the Valley of Mexico, which at its height held perhaps 100,000 people or more, one of the largest cities in the world at the time. Laid out along a grand avenue, it influenced much of Mesoamerica before it declined and its centre was burned.
spans.note: Who built it is unknown; the name is the Aztecs'. Population estimates run 100,000–200,000.
spans.significance: Teotihuacan's trade, architecture and political reach shaped Mesoamerica for centuries; in 378 CE a Teotihuacan-backed warlord installed a new dynasty at the Maya city of Tikal. Centuries after its fall, the Aztecs revered its ruins as the place where the gods had created the sun.

spans.name: Three Kingdoms of China
spans.description: The period after the fall of the Han dynasty when China was divided among three rival states: Wei in the north, Shu in the southwest and Wu in the southeast. It ended when the Jin dynasty, which had replaced Wei, conquered Wu and reunified China.
spans.note: 220 (Cao Pi ends the Han) to 280 (Jin conquers Wu); some accounts start the era with the wars of 184 or 208.
spans.significance: Though marked by long wars and a steep fall in registered population, the period became one of the most celebrated in Chinese culture through the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Its heroes, such as Zhuge Liang and Guan Yu, remain famous across East Asia in opera, film and games.

links.why: Hammurabi's laws continued the Mesopotamian tradition of written codes with set penalties seen first at Ur.
Hatshepsut ruled in the New Kingdom's Eighteenth Dynasty.
Akhenaten's Amarna period fell within the New Kingdom's Eighteenth Dynasty.
Ramesses II fought at Kadesh to defend Egypt's empire in the Levant.
The inscriptions record the divinations of Shang kings, beginning with Wu Ding.
The destruction of Troy VIIa is usually counted among the Late Bronze Age destructions; the legend is harder to date.
With bronze trade networks broken, iron, smelted from more common ores, came into wider use; historians debate how much.
Carthage grew into the western Mediterranean power that later fought Rome in the Punic Wars.
The Ptolemies' patronage funded the Mouseion and its library in their new capital.
As the library's chief librarian, Eratosthenes worked with its records and scholarship.
The sisters rose against the Han governor of Jiaozhi and drove his forces out.
The pyramid was Teotihuacan's largest monument, on its main avenue.
Teotihuacan's trade and styles reached the Maya, and in 378 it backed a new dynasty at Tikal.
The Aztecs revered its ruins as sacred and borrowed its imagery and objects.
When Cao Pi deposed the last Han emperor, China split among Wei, Shu and Wu.
Jin's conquest of Wu ended the division and reunified China.
